links.took: Single-screen two-player Atari 2600 head-to-head positioning and point-scoring duels.
links.added: Replaced tank and biplane gunfights with overhead ring footwork, jabs, and timed knockouts in Activision's launch lineup.
links.extra: Designed by Activision co-founder Bob Whitehead as one of the company's first four cartridges in July 1980.

links.took: Arcade-paced boxing focused on reading an opponent's guard, timing quick punches, and chasing knockdowns.
links.added: Shifted from an overhead two-player ring to a behind-the-boxer perspective against oversized, telegraphing arcade rivals.
links.extra: Early milestone showing boxing timing could work cleanly with simple digital inputs.

links.took: Four-gear shifting discipline and split-second acceleration control from Atari's early arcade racers.
links.added: Distilled racing into a straight-line quarter-mile drag strip where missed shifts blow the engine and runs are chased to hundredths of a second.
links.extra: Created by David Crane as Activision's very first commercial release in 1980.

links.took: David Crane's tight Atari 2600 kernel timing and crisp frame-level input responsiveness for Activision.
links.added: Expanded a single-screen racing test into a 255-screen horizontal jungle adventure with animated vine-swinging.
links.extra: Both titles were written by Activision co-founder David Crane on the Atari 2600.

links.took: Splitting space rocks and escalating wave danger from Atari's vector shooter.
links.added: Grounded the player's laser cannon along a planetary floor to intercept falling meteors, spinners, and guided bombs while deducting points for missed rocks.
links.extra: Programmed by John Sohl for Mattel Electronics; became one of the Intellivision's best-selling cartridges.

links.took: Horizontal bottom-edge laser defense under relentless waves descending from the top of the screen.
links.added: Added autofire, hyperspace teleporting, and variable-speed falling hazards with progressive color-coded background stages.
links.extra: Originally conceived as a hybrid of Asteroids and Missile Command under the working title Meteor!

links.took: Swooping alien birds that divide into smaller attackers and fire angled laser streams down at a mobile turret.
links.added: Delivered shimmering multicolored Atari 2600 sprite patterns and undulating formations across escalating planetary skies.
links.extra: Programmed by Rob Fulop for Imagic; Atari sued over its similarity to Phoenix before settling out of court.

links.took: Ten-event track-and-field decathlon structure testing sprinting, jumping, and throwing disciplines in sequence.
links.added: Brought frantic joystick-waggling speed trials and multi-event scoring onto the Atari 2600 with Activision's animated runner sprites.
links.extra: Designed by David Crane in 1983 and notorious for snapping Atari CX40 joysticks.

links.took: Ten-event track-and-field marathon combining rapid alternating inputs with timed jumps and throws.
links.added: Married Activision's decathlon format with Konami's arcade pacing for a massively popular British home-computer showcase.

src.t: Retro Gamer: The Making of Daley Thompson's Decathlon

links.extra: Ocean Software's 1984 hit turned keyboard-bashing sports marathons into a UK playground staple.

links.took: Behind-the-car horizon-scaling road perspective and dodging slower rival cars at high speed.
links.added: Brought pseudo-3D road racing to the Atari 2600 while adding continuous day-to-night transitions, fog, ice, and multi-day pass quotas.
links.extra: Programmed by Larry Miller for Activision, widely praised as one of the Atari 2600's deepest racers.

links.took: Hopping across horizontally drifting rows of moving hazards while racing a ticking timer.
links.added: Inverted crossing a river into jumping repeatedly across Arctic ice floes to turn them blue and construct an igloo block by block before freezing.
links.extra: Designed by Steve Cartwright at Activision in 1983.

links.took: Activision's multi-screen subterranean Atari 2600 cavern exploration with vertical shaft navigation.
links.added: Equipped the rescuer with a backpack helicopter, laser helmet, and limited dynamite charges to blast rock walls and save trapped miners before power runs out.
links.extra: Created by John Van Ryzin at Activision's East Coast studio in 1984.

links.took: Subterranean descent combining limited wall-blasting bombs, dark cavern navigation, and rescuing trapped survivors.
links.added: Transformed fixed cavern stages into procedurally generated roguelike mines with whip combat, physics traps, and shops.
links.extra: H.E.R.O. pioneered the bomb-and-rescue underground exploration loop revisited decades later by modern indie cave platformers.

links.took: Shielded horizontal cannon shooting marching alien rows in its opening Astro Battles wave.
links.added: Chained five distinct shooter missions—including diving formations, warp tunnels, and a destructible flagship—inside one talking arcade cabinet.
links.extra: Designed by Jamie Fenton at Dave Nutting Associates for Midway with an early Votrax speech synthesizer.

links.took: Swooping, multicolored alien squadrons peeling out of formation to bomb the player's ship.
links.added: Embedded a full Galaxian-style mission directly inside a multi-genre space-shooter progression loop with escalating rank titles.
links.extra: Bally Midway originally had to omit a planned Galaxian trademark reference after licensing shifts.

links.took: Clearing a fixed-screen arcade maze of dots while evading four pursuing enemies on tight corner turns.
links.added: Added green revolving turnstile doors players flip to dynamically reshape corridors, plus timed bonus letters spelling EXTRA and SPECIAL.
links.extra: Released by Universal in 1981 and celebrated on ColecoVision as one of the finest maze-chase evolutions.

links.took: Konami's horizontally scrolling cavern flight balancing forward shots, gravity bombs, and depleting fuel.
links.added: Swapped the rocket for an agile helicopter across ten distinct terrain sectors ending with airlifting a loot box from the final base.
links.extra: Direct arcade sequel released by Konami just months after Scramble in 1981.

links.took: Single-screen vertical ladder climbing across multi-tiered platforms while outrunning patrolling arcade foes.
links.added: Replaced jumping over barrels with walking across oversized burger buns and patties to drop them onto chasing Mr. Hot Dog and Mr. Egg enemies.
links.extra: Created by Data East in 1982 (originally Hamburger in Japan) with a limited pepper stun mechanic.

links.took: General Computer Corporation's lively arcade chase pacing, crisp risk-reward scoring, and personality-packed enemies.
links.added: Replaced walled dot mazes with an open analog-stick plaza where Charley Chuck pelts four chasing chefs with pies before his ice-cream cone melts.
links.extra: GCC's first original arcade game for Atari after developing Ms. Pac-Man.

links.took: Single-screen arcade corridor pursuit inside a compact rectangular arena with corner-turning tension.
links.added: Made the maze walls pushable ice blocks that slide to crush Sno-Bee enemies or align three diamond blocks for massive point bonuses.
links.extra: Developed by Coreland and published by Sega in 1982; famous for its upbeat 'Popcorn' soundtrack.

links.took: Shigeru Miyamoto's multi-tier arcade rescue structure originally conceived around King Features' Popeye love triangle.
links.added: Realized the official Popeye license without a jump button, instead punching incoming hazards, collecting Olive Oyl's falling hearts, and eating spinach to knock Brutus off-screen.
links.extra: Co-developed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Genyo Takeda in 1982; later became one of three Famicom launch titles in 1983.

links.took: Williams' high-speed Motorola 6809 arcade engineering and long-range radar tracking across wrap-around space.
links.added: Replaced horizontal humanoid rescues with 360-degree 49-way joystick asteroid mining to build Sinibombs before a howling, voice-synthesized boss constructs itself and hunts the player.
links.extra: Created at Williams Electronics by Noah Falstein, Sam Dicker, RJ Mical, Jack Haeger, and John Newcomer.

links.took: Free-floating multidirectional space combat weaving through drifting rock fields.
links.added: Turned shooting asteroids into a frantic resource race—harvesting glowing crystals for Sinibombs while worker drones mine the same rocks to assemble the Sinistar.
links.extra: Introduced digitized snarling voice taunts ('Beware, I live!' / 'Run, coward!') that defined arcade dread.

links.took: Omnidirectional scrolling space dogfighting with free 360-degree flight rather than a locked scroll direction.
links.added: Stripped away obstacle corridors in favor of endless parallax cloud layers and jumping across five eras from 1910 biplanes to 2001 UFOs.
links.extra: Designed by Yoshiki Okamoto at Konami in 1982.

links.took: Yoshiki Okamoto's fast-paced Konami arcade shooting cadence and dramatic wave escalation.
links.added: Pivoted open-sky 360-degree flying into a circular perimeter rail firing toward a central deep-space vanishing point.
links.extra: Yoshiki Okamoto designed both Time Pilot (1982) and Gyruss (1983) at Konami.

links.took: Yoshiki Okamoto's WWII aerial combat pacing, enemy squadrons, and arcade accessibility.
links.added: Carried his sky-dogfighting instincts from Konami to Capcom, framing a vertical Pacific-theater shooter with barrel-roll dodges aimed squarely at Western arcades.
links.extra: Okamoto left Konami after Time Pilot and Gyruss to join Capcom, where he directed 1942.

links.took: Dot-collecting maze chases cleared by sweeping every pickup off the board while evading patrolling foes.
links.added: Projected Bentley Bear's gem hunt onto trimetric 3D castles with trackball control, jumps, secret warps, and a true game ending.

src.t: Franz Lanzinger, Classic Game Postmortem: Crystal Castles (GDC Vault)

links.extra: Creator Franz Lanzinger explicitly described Crystal Castles as 'really just 3D Pac-Man'.

links.took: Pseudo-3D diagonal arcade projection giving flat raster screens an immediate sense of stepped elevation.
links.added: Expanded a single pyramid into ten richly layered multi-level castles with staircases, elevators, honey pots, and enemies that also eat remaining gems.
links.extra: Released by Atari in 1983 as one of the first arcade games with a finite final stage and ending screen.

links.took: Multi-floor arcade climbing across stacked platforms while dodging hazards and timing vertical transitions.
links.added: Turned climbing into a 30-story scrolling spy infiltration with working elevators, shootable ceiling lights, crouching gunfights, and red document doors.
links.extra: Released by Taito in 1983 and widely ported to home consoles and Dendy multicarts.

links.took: Namco's bright, character-driven single-screen arcade chase polish and playful risk-reward enemy traps.
links.added: Replaced underground tunneling with horizontally scrolling mansion burglaries, color-coded breakable trampolines, and microwave-blast doors.
links.extra: Ran on Namco's Super Pac-Man arcade hardware in 1983 and became a beloved Famicom staple.

links.took: Nintendo R&D1's dual-screen Multi Screen LCD clamshell format built for pocket reflex play.
links.added: Hinged the two screens side by side like a book so Mario and Luigi pass bottles back and forth across tiered factory conveyor belts.

src.t: Wikipedia: List of Game & Watch games

links.extra: Debuted Luigi in March 1983—months before the arcade Mario Bros. cabinet shipped.

links.took: Single-screen ladder-and-jump arcade pursuit with leaping across stacked ledges to reach a partner.
links.added: Packed 50 fruit-gathering puzzle-platform stages and a built-in Edit Mode onto the Famicom's very first third-party cartridge.
links.extra: Developed by Hudson Soft in 1983 and ported to Famicom in July 1984.

links.took: Konami's multi-event arcade structure chaining distinct short timing trials into one continuous score attack.
links.added: Replaced Olympic athletics with six colorful circus acts—lion fire-hoop leaps, monkey tightropes, bouncing balls, and flying trapezes.
links.extra: Konami's 1984 arcade hit became ubiquitous across NES, MSX, and Eastern European Dendy multicarts.

links.took: Wrap-around arcade platforming built around timing jumps, dodging patrolling foes, and scoring chain bonuses.
links.added: Added horizontal wrap-around scrolling where leading a long conga line of rescued Chirps to the exit multiplies points while dodging prowling Tiger cats.
links.extra: Designed by Yoji Ishii at Sega in 1984.

links.took: Sega's iconic blue Flicky birds and their core motif of rescuing tiny animals trapped by enemies.
links.added: Placed Flickies directly inside Dr. Robotnik's Badniks so smashing robots releases bouncing blue birds across Sonic's high-speed stages.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.extra: Sonic Team later brought the entire Flicky premise into 3D in Sonic 3D: Flickies' Island.

links.took: Nintendo R&D1's NES Zapper light-gun optical target detection and rapid-fire arcade scoring.
links.added: Swapped flying ducks for rotating cardboard mobsters mixed with innocent bystanders, punishing players who shoot civilians in Trick Shot and street modes.
links.extra: Co-created by Nintendo R&D1 alongside Duck Hunt and Wild Gunman as a Zapper showcase in 1984.

links.took: Top-down vertical-scrolling high-speed highway dodging through dense traffic and narrowing roadways.
links.added: Added a responsive counter-steering skid recovery mechanic, fuel-replenishing rainbow cars, and six varied stretches from bridges to coastal cliffs.
links.extra: Konami's 1984 arcade racer was hugely popular on Famicom, MSX, and Dendy.

links.took: Single-screen ladder-climbing grid puzzles paired with an integrated player-accessible stage editor.
links.added: Replaced digging holes with Mario swinging a demolition hammer to shatter brick walls, detonate chain-reaction bombs, and trap enemies without jumping.
links.extra: Directed by Yoshio Sakamoto at Nintendo R&D1 in 1985 ahead of Metroid.

links.took: Mario and Luigi's blue-collar arcade world, alternating two-player runs, and grounded character sprites.
links.added: Cast the brothers as demolition workers battling Foreman Spike across 100 destructible architectural puzzle phases.
links.extra: Introduced Foreman Spike, who returned decades later in the 2023 Super Mario Bros. Movie.

links.took: Dodging speeding multi-lane street traffic to cross a busy highway without getting flattened.
links.added: Used the road crossing as an opener to rent skis before launching into a second downhill slalom racing event.

src.t: Retro Gamer: The Story of Horace

links.extra: Created by William Tang for Beam Software / Melbourne House in 1982; starred the ZX Spectrum's earliest mascot.

links.took: Vertical downhill slalom steering between paired gate flags while weaving around trees and moguls.
links.added: Paired the downhill ski run with an arcade traffic-crossing prelude and cash-balance ski rentals on the ZX Spectrum.
links.extra: Showcased multi-stage arcade variety on early 16K Sinclair ZX Spectrum hardware.

links.took: First-person forward-scrolling scaling visuals conveying breakneck speed through oncoming roadside markers.
links.added: Replaced empty highway pylons with a dense ZX Spectrum forest where players weave a laser-armed motorbike between rushing trees to shoot fleeing bikers.
links.extra: Programmed by Mervyn Estcourt for Micromega in 1983; ranked #1 in Your Sinclair's Top 100 Spectrum games.

links.took: Diagonal isometric projection creating convincing three-dimensional architecture on modest 8-bit hardware.
links.added: Built a full rotatable 3D walled city on ZX Spectrum letting players choose a boy or girl hero to throw grenades and rescue their partner from giant ants.

src.t: Retro Gamer: The Making of Ant Attack

links.extra: Created by sculptor and programmer Sandy White for Quicksilva in 1983.

links.took: Free-roaming isometric 3D movement and height-layered block environments on the Sinclair ZX Spectrum.
links.added: Pioneered masked sprite occlusion inside Ultimate's Filmation engine so characters cleanly walked behind walls and stacked objects.
links.extra: Ant Attack's 'Softsolid' 3D city proved isometric worlds worked on 8-bit micros one year before Knight Lore.

links.took: Ultimate Play the Game's jetpack-flying astronaut, crisp horizontal laser beams, and relentless alien swarms.
links.added: Expanded a single-screen rocket build into a horizontally scrolling lunar surface with a drivable Moon Rover, portable bridge kits, and teleporters.
links.extra: Second title in Ultimate's Jetman series by Tim and Chris Stamper in 1983.

links.took: Eugene Jarvis's frantic bidirectional scrolling, top-edge radar scanner, smart bombs, and humanoid rescues.
links.added: Grew directly out of Archer Maclean's aborted Atari 8-bit Defender and Stargate conversion prototypes, starring a jetpack hero defending Io's scientists.

src.t: Games That Weren't: Archer Maclean's Lost Defender & Stargate Conversions

links.extra: Archival disks confirmed Maclean's Defender/Stargate Atari 8-bit prototypes directly birthed Dropzone in 1984.

links.took: Compact ZX Spectrum side-view platform navigation through vividly drawn British everyday settings.
links.added: Abandoned lethal platforming traps for a living, schedule-driven schoolyard simulation with autonomous teachers, class timetables, catapult pranks, and cracking the headmaster's safe.
links.extra: Designed by David Reidy for Microsphere in 1984.

links.took: Interactive schoolyard sandbox governed by class schedules, patrolling authority figures, student cliques, and mischievous pranks.
links.added: Translated the rebellious boarding-school ecosystem into Rockstar's 3D open-world action-adventure framework two decades later.

src.t: The Guardian: Skool Daze and Bully

links.extra: Retrospective critics widely credit Skool Daze as the 8-bit ancestor of Rockstar's Bully.

links.took: Julian Gollop's turn-based ZX Spectrum grid positioning, line-of-sight rules, and tense tactical combat.
links.added: Cast up to eight competing wizards in a magical arena featuring probabilistic spellcasting, summonable illusions opponents can disbelieve, and a shifting Law/Chaos balance.

src.t: Wikipedia: Chaos: The Battle of Wizards
MobyGames: Chaos: The Battle of Wizards

links.extra: Designed by Julian Gollop and published by Games Workshop in 1985.

links.took: Julian Gollop's mastery of turn-based probability, morale tension, and multi-unit tactical interplay.
links.added: Brought those crisp turn-based combat calculations into squad-level sci-fi skirmishes with action points and hidden enemy movement.

src.t: Wikipedia: Chaos: The Battle of Wizards

links.extra: Julian Gollop's direct stepping stone from Rebelstar and Chaos to Laser Squad and UFO: Enemy Unknown.

links.took: Multi-room stealth infiltration under a countdown timer while dodging security cameras and searching terminals.
links.added: Infused the warehouse raid with martial-arts ninja kicks, collectible shurikens and bricks, guard dogs, and an escaping rooftop helicopter climax.

src.t: Retro Gamer: The Making of Saboteur

links.extra: Solo-created by Clive Townsend for Durell Software in 1985.

links.took: Masked isometric 3D interior rooms and object-carrying puzzle exploration popularized on UK 8-bit computers.
links.added: Set the isometric world inside a WWII POW camp governed by automated guard patrols, roll calls, and meal schedules that play out even if the player stands still.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Great Escape (1986 video game)
Retro Gamer: The Making of The Great Escape

links.extra: Developed by Denton Designs and published by Ocean Software in 1986.

links.took: Real-time 3D polygonal spatial awareness on constrained British 8-bit home computers.
links.added: Moved past wireframe spaceships to solid-filled 3D terraced landscapes where players absorb energy, build boulders, and teleport upward to out-elevate a rotating Sentinel.
links.extra: Created by Geoff Crammond for Firebird in 1986 (released as The Sentry in the US).

links.took: Geoff Crammond's ultra-efficient solid-filled 3D polygon rendering routines and spatial physics craft.
links.added: Applied Crammond's custom 3D polygon tech to rollercoaster-like elevated stunt tracks with responsive suspension physics on Amiga and Atari ST.
links.extra: Geoff Crammond wrote The Sentinel (1986), Stunt Car Racer (1989), and Formula One Grand Prix (1991).

links.took: Rotational ship thrust, gravity management, and fuel conservation while threading narrow rocky chasms.
links.added: Combined cave-skimming inertia with laser gunfights against turrets and towing a heavy reactor pod suspended on a physics-simulated tractor beam.
links.extra: Designed by Jeremy Smith for Firebird in 1986, inspiring a wave of gravity-cave shooters.

links.took: Isometric 3D exploration inside a strict institutional schedule where breaking daily routine triggers suspicion.
links.added: Transposed the formula to a fourteenth-century monastery inspired by Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose, with canonical hours, an AI novice follower, and a murder mystery.

src.t: Retro Gamer: La Abadia del Crimen

links.extra: Programmed by Paco Menendez with art by Juan Delcan for Opera Soft in 1987; widely hailed as Spain's 8-bit magnum opus.

links.took: Masked 3D isometric room architecture that defined European 8-bit adventure visuals.
links.added: Pushed 8-bit isometric design to dramatic cloister arches, multi-angle room cameras, and narrative detective deductions.
links.extra: Originally developed in Spain for Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, MSX, and DOS.

links.took: Kevin Toms' foundational British soccer management loop balancing league tables, squad selection, and animated match highlights.
links.added: Added player transfer auctions, sponsorship deals, training boosts, and multi-screen tactical pitch setup.
links.extra: Sequel by original creator Kevin Toms for Addictive Games in 1988.

links.took: Menu-driven British club management focused on transfers, squad fitness, and long-term league promotion.
links.added: Dropped simple arcade highlights for Paul and Oliver Collyer's deep database-driven text commentary and realistic player ratings.
links.extra: Bridged Addictive Games' 1980s management boom and Sports Interactive's modern sim lineage.

links.took: The Oliver Twins' somersaulting egg hero and item-swapping environmental adventure puzzles.
links.added: Cemented the classic Dizzy blueprint by adding three lives, an energy bar, interactive NPC dialogue, and a fairy-tale quest to rescue Daisy.
links.extra: Third entry in Codemasters' hugely popular UK budget adventure-platformer series.

links.took: Turn-based sci-fi hex-grid wargaming focused on combined-arms unit counters, factories, and terrain bonuses.
links.added: Brought the format to Amiga and DOS with an innovative split-screen phase system where one player moves while the other executes combat orders.
links.extra: Developed by German studio Blue Byte in 1991, explicitly drawing from Hudson's Nectaris/Military Madness.

links.took: Blue Byte's polished Amiga PC strategy engineering, crisp tile art, and deep German systems-design ethos.
links.added: Shifted from turn-based hex warfare to real-time medieval supply-chain logistics and bustling autonomous villagers.
links.extra: Battle Isle established Blue Byte as Europe's premier PC strategy developer ahead of The Settlers.

links.took: Brightly themed console platform worlds stuffed with secret rooms, power-up traversal, and playful enemy variety.
links.added: Turned Chris Sorrell's fish agent into a stretchy, endlessly telescoping bionic hero navigating Santa's toy factory in drivable planes and bathtubs.
links.extra: Developed by Vectordean / Millennium in 1991; one of the defining Amiga and Mega Drive European platformers.

links.took: Eugene Jarvis's relentless twin-stick arena shooting, waving swarms, human rescues, and shattering particle explosions.
links.added: Born from Jeff Minter coding Robotron's signature slivering explosions on the Atari ST, replacing humanoids with sheep across 100 surreal shareware waves.

src.t: Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story / Codetapper Interview

links.extra: Minter called Robotron: 2084 'the purest, most aggressive and challenging videogame ever made'.

links.took: Jeff Minter's hypnotic particle bursts, blistering arcade intensity, and pulsing rave soundtrack sensibility.
links.added: Transplanted that psychedelic Llamasoft arcade energy onto Atari's 3D vector-web classic for the Atari Jaguar.
links.extra: Llamatron's shareware success directly preceded Atari commissioning Minter for Tempest 2000.

links.took: Relentless side-scrolling single-plane combat against waves of rushing grunts culminating in stage bosses.
links.added: Swapped martial-arts strikes for a Cold War commando wielding a combat knife alongside stolen flamethrowers, bazookas, and grenades.
links.extra: Released by Konami in 1985 as Green Beret internationally and Rush'n Attack in North America.

links.took: Konami's lethal one-hit-kill military side-scrolling pacing across enemy bases and armored hazards.
links.added: Added eight-directional gunfire, leaping somersaults, spread-gun power-ups, and simultaneous two-player arcade co-op.
links.extra: Bridged Konami's melee-focused commando action and its iconic 1987 run-and-gun revolution.

links.took: Horizontal scrolling starfighter shooting built around progressive weapon power-ups and memorable mechanical setpieces.
links.added: Stretched the battlefield across an unprecedented triple-screen arcade cabinet featuring branching stage paths and giant cybernetic fish bosses.
links.extra: Taito's 1986 cabinet used mirrors to join three CRT monitors seamlessly into an ultra-wide aspect ratio.

links.took: Exaggerated arcade basketball spectacle featuring dramatic close-up slam-dunk animations that interrupt live court play.
links.added: Elevated over-the-top hoops into digitized 2-on-2 NBA showdowns with flaming balls, shattering glass, and booming play-by-play commentary.
links.extra: Konami's 1986 arcade/NES hit pioneered cinematic slam-dunk cutscenes in basketball games.

links.took: Konami's crisp arcade sports timing, vibrant digitized speech calls, and competitive two-player pacing.
links.added: Applied Konami's arcade sports polish to full-court five-on-five basketball with timed shot-release jumps and animated dunk cutscenes.
links.extra: Released in arcades in 1986 and became one of the NES's signature sports cartridges.

links.took: Vertical overhead military shoot-'em-up raids advancing through fortified jungles, trenches, and enemy bunkers.
links.added: Put two co-op players behind the wheel of armed jeeps crashing through prison camps to rescue POWs and deliver them to extraction choppers.
links.extra: Konami's 1986 arcade hit (Top Gunner in North America) became an iconic NES and Dendy co-op classic.

links.took: Espionage gunfights utilizing background doors for tactical cover and methodical room-by-room progression.
links.added: Shifted the secret-agent action horizontally across two-tier walkways with scarce bullets replenished by ducking into marked ammo doors.
links.extra: Developed by Namco in 1986 on Namco System 86 hardware.

links.took: Multi-tier side-scrolling operative action emphasizing deliberate jumps between upper and lower walkways while clearing armed henchmen.
links.added: Recast the spy as ninja Joe Musashi with infinite shurikens, auto-triggering melee slashes, hostage rescues, and first-person bonus stages.
links.extra: Widely recognized by arcade historians as Sega's direct martial-arts answer to Namco's Rolling Thunder.

links.took: Demanding mythic side-scrolling arcade action packed with relentless enemies and escalating obstacle courses.
links.added: Equipped the Legendary Warrior with a chained yo-yo-like Diskarmor shield and later reimagined the NES release as an interconnected action-RPG.
links.extra: Tecmo's 1986 arcade hit was famously expanded into a non-linear exploration adventure on NES.

links.took: Single-screen action-puzzle stages requiring players to manipulate tile geometry to trap enemies and reach objectives.
links.added: Inverted digging holes in floors into conjuring and shattering magic stone blocks mid-air to build pathways to each chamber's key and exit door.
links.extra: Created by Michitaka Tsuruta at Tecmo in 1986; later spawned prequel Fire 'n Ice.

links.took: Capcom's vertical WWII Pacific-theater starfighter action with enemy formations and evasive barrel rolls.
links.added: Replaced one-hit lives with a continuously draining fuel gauge, selectable timed weapons, lightning screen-clearers, and towering battleship bosses like the Yamato.
links.extra: Directed by Yoshiki Okamoto at Capcom in 1987.

links.took: Top-down cooperative maze shooting navigating locked doors and relentless monster waves.
links.added: Swapped fantasy dungeons for claustrophobic sci-fi horror ships where two soldiers rescue hostages under a ticking time bomb before fighting grotesque bio-bosses.
links.extra: Released by Sega in 1987 on System 16 arcade hardware and ported widely to Master System and NES.

links.took: Konami's crisp arcade sports presentation, digitized voice announcements, and kinetic two-player NES competition.
links.added: Brought the formula to ice hockey with smooth rink scrolling, passing arrows, shootout tiebreakers, and mid-game fistfights where only the loser goes to the penalty box.
links.extra: Konami's 1987 arcade/NES hockey classic even hid a playable Gradius mini-game during intermission.

links.took: Fast-paced arcade ice hockey combining smooth rink action, fighting interludes, and lively crowd energy.
links.added: Scaled console hockey into EA's 16-bit vertically scrolling Genesis simulator with official NHL teams and realistic passing physics.
links.extra: Set the 8-bit benchmark for accessible, hard-hitting hockey before EA launched its NHL dynasty.

links.took: Behind-the-car horizon-scaling sports-car racing across scenic sunset highways with selectable music tracks.
links.added: Pushed Nasir Gebelli's 6502 line-scrolling wizardry onto the NES with Ferrari-inspired styling and a toggleable anaglyph 3D glasses mode.

src.t: Automaton: Hironobu Sakaguchi & Nasir Gebelli Retrospective

links.extra: Directed by Hironobu Sakaguchi and programmed by Nasir Gebelli at Square in 1987.

links.took: The core Square quartet of Hironobu Sakaguchi, Nasir Gebelli, Nobuo Uematsu, and Kazuko Shibuya collaborating under tight 8-bit deadlines.
links.added: Channeled that same team's NES technical command and musical polish directly into Square's make-or-break role-playing landmark months later.

src.t: Game Developer: Nasir Gebelli & Final Fantasy History

links.extra: Released just months before Final Fantasy in 1987 by the same core Square staff.

links.took: Yu Suzuki's hydraulic sit-down motorcycle arcade racer utilizing Sega's Super Scaler sprite-zooming roads.
links.added: Added four difficulty-tiered continental courses, a 324 km/h turbo boost button, and Out Run-style selectable rock tracks.
links.extra: Released by Sega AM2 in 1987 and later enhanced with an original career-upgrade mode on Mega Drive.

links.took: Cooperative two-player street brawling punching and kicking waves of urban thugs across scrolling stages.
links.added: Collapsed depth-plane movement into two crisp Shinobi-style vertical tiers set atop moving semi-trucks, trains, and sewers to rescue President Ronnie.
links.extra: Data East's 1988 arcade brawler achieved cult fame for its opening 'Are you a bad enough dude?' screen.

links.took: Square's four-character turn-based fantasy RPG structure, side-view battle layout, and world-spanning airship quests.
links.added: Replaced traditional experience levels with usage-based stat growth, keyword-memory dialogue, named protagonists, Chocobos, and Cid.
links.extra: Directed by Hironobu Sakaguchi with Akitoshi Kawazu designing its experimental skill-growth system in 1988.

links.took: Yu Suzuki's Sega Super Scaler road-zooming speed and vibrant arcade spectacle.
links.added: Leapt onto Sega's Y Board with roller-coaster banked tracks, looping jumps, 12 distinct drivers, and frantic 12-buggy pack racing.
links.extra: Designed by Yu Suzuki and Sega AM2 in 1988 inside a tilting hydraulic arcade cabinet.

links.took: Colorful multi-character buggy racing across tight, playful circuits populated by quirky mascot drivers.
links.added: Replaced sprite-scaled hills with Mode 7 flat-plane kart drifting, item boxes, split-screen multiplayer, and Battle Mode.
links.extra: Demonstrated arcade mascot buggy racing four years before Super Mario Kart defined the kart-racer genre.

links.took: Single-plane side-scrolling arcade combat clearing waves of oncoming monsters with punches, kicks, and crouches.
links.added: Drenched the brawler in slasher-film horror gore, wieldable cleavers and shotguns, and a hockey-masked hero fighting through a cursed mansion.
links.extra: Namco's 1988 arcade hit became the first game to carry an explicit parental advisory warning on its TurboGrafx-16 box.

links.took: Konami's relentless two-player co-op run-and-gun action, eight-way aiming, and screen-filling alien bosses.
links.added: Swapped behind-the-back base corridors for overhead top-down assault stages, stackable weapon upgrades, and tighter jump control.
links.extra: Released in arcades in 1988 and popularized worldwide on NES as Super C.

links.took: Open-ended top-down labyrinth exploration collecting keys, health upgrades, and special sub-weapons across an interconnected map.
links.added: Interwove Zelda-style on-foot adventure rooms seamlessly with high-speed vertical shoot-'em-up corridor stages where the heroine transforms into a starfighter.
links.extra: Developed by Compile in 1988 (Guardic Gaiden in Japan) for the NES.

links.took: Compile's blistering vertical shoot-'em-up action, numbered special weapons, and intense boss choreography.
links.added: Embedded Compile's signature overhead shooter stages inside a full-fledged top-down sci-fi adventure world.
links.extra: Both Zanac (1986) and The Guardian Legend (1988) were created by Compile.

links.took: Crisp NES side-scrolling ninja agility built around wall-clinging, rhythmic vertical wall jumps, and cinematic cutscenes.
links.added: Paired rapid wall-kick ascents with three switchable Bat-weapons (Batarang, Spear Gun, Dirk) across dark, atmospheric Gotham stages.
links.extra: Developed by Sunsoft in 1989 with a landmark bass-heavy NES chiptune score by Naoki Kodaka.

links.took: Compile's dynamic AI difficulty adjustment, multi-level numbered weapon capsules, and relentless vertical bullet speed.
links.added: Showcased the TurboGrafx-16's 16-bit sprite power with layered parallax starfields, homing-missile combos, and marathon boss gauntlets.
links.extra: Developed by Compile and published by Hudson Soft in 1989 (Gunhed in Japan).

links.took: Konami's signature horizontal power-meter shooting bar, laser beams, and floating Option pods.
links.added: Added four preset weapon configurations, a full custom Edit Mode arsenal builder, 3D pseudo-corridor bonus stages, and notorious arcade difficulty.
links.extra: Released by Konami in arcades in 1989 and widely acclaimed via its rebalanced 1990 SNES launch port.

links.took: Single-screen two-player cooperative arcade clearing packed with bouncing targets, fruit bonuses, and tight platform layouts.
links.added: Replaced bubble-trapping dragons with vertical harpoons fired straight upward to split giant bouncing balloons into ever-smaller halves across world landmarks.
links.extra: Created by Mitchell Corporation in 1989 (Buster Bros. in North America, Pang in Europe and Japan).

links.took: Sega's lethal one-hit arcade ninja action, multi-level walkways, shurikens, and hostage rescues.
links.added: Introduced a loyal white wolf companion commanded to lunge and pin down armed enemies while the ninja defuses time bombs.
links.extra: Released by Sega in arcades in 1989; its 1990 Mega Drive counterpart featured completely redesigned stages.

links.took: Methodical horizontal arcade shooting centered around mastering a multi-purpose front-mounted ship attachment.
links.added: Replaced R-Type's Force Pod with a tractor beam that grabs live enemy ships to absorb shots as shields or hurl back as projectiles.
links.extra: Developed by Toaplan in 1989; its 1991 European Mega Drive intro later birthed the 'All your base are belong to us' internet meme.

links.took: Toaplan's razor-sharp arcade bullet patterns, color-coded weapon pickups, and high-speed checkpoint structure.
links.added: Pivoted Toaplan's trademark vertical arcade shooter craft into a sleek horizontal space opera with enemy-capture tactics.
links.extra: Both titles showcase Toaplan's late-1980s arcade shoot-'em-up engineering.

links.took: Capcom's CPS-1 arcade belt-scrolling brawler engine, huge animated sprites, and snappy punch-grab combos.
links.added: Doubled co-op capacity to four simultaneous players while adding running dash strikes, rideable combat mechs, and a sci-fi superhero quartet.
links.extra: Released by Capcom in 1991 on CPS-1 hardware starring Capcom's longtime promotional mascot.

links.took: Sega's sword-and-sorcery belt-scrolling hack-and-slash action featuring Ax Battler, Tyris Flare, Gilius, and rideable beasts.
links.added: Added charge-controlled partial magic casting, backward spinning attacks, new lizard mounts, and a dedicated survival Duel mode on Mega Drive.
links.extra: Developed exclusively for the Sega Mega Drive / Genesis in 1991.

links.took: Capcom's CPS-1 side-scrolling beat-'em-up cadence, crowd control, and directional special attacks.
links.added: Introduced Arthurian sword-and-shield blocking, rideable warhorses, and an RPG-style experience bar that visibly upgrades armor and weapons across 16 levels.

src.t: Wikipedia: Knights of the Round (video game)

links.extra: Released by Capcom on CPS-1 in 1991, bridging arcade brawlers and fantasy RPG progression.

links.took: Fast-paced falling-piece clearing inside a narrow vertical well where rising stacks end the game.
links.added: Swapped rotating tetrominoes for swapping four bottom stacks to sandwich Mario enemies between matching Yoshi eggshells and hatch bonus Yoshis.
links.extra: Developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo in 1991 (titled Yoshi in North America and Mario & Yoshi in Europe).

links.took: Game Freak's Nintendo-published commercial success and tight collaboration among Satoshi Tajiri, Ken Sugimori, and Junichi Masuda.
links.added: Funded Game Freak through its six-year development of Pokémon Red and Green while cementing its relationship with Nintendo.
links.extra: Directed by Satoshi Tajiri with music by Junichi Masuda and character art by Ken Sugimori.

links.took: First-person grid-based dungeon crawling managing a multi-character party through turn-based labyrinth combat.
links.added: Brought step-based dungeon exploration to the 16-bit Mega Drive with smooth corridor animations, expressive enemy sprites, and an intuitive icon-ring menu.
links.extra: Co-developed by Climax Entertainment and Sonic! Software Planning in 1991.

links.took: Sega's Shining fantasy setting, expressive battle portraits, and four-direction icon menu system.
links.added: Pivoted the franchise from first-person dungeon corridors into sweeping turn-based tactical grid warfare with dozens of recruitable heroes.
links.extra: Launched Sega's flagship 16-bit RPG series before Climax pivoted it into tactical RPGs.

links.took: Westone's side-scrolling action-RPG structure linking towns, gear shops, and magical exploration abilities.
links.added: Shifted onto 16-bit Mega Drive hardware with an interconnected human-hero quest, spear-and-sword reach options, and AI fairy and dragon companions.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wonder Boy in Monster World
MobyGames: Wonder Boy in Monster World

links.extra: Fifth entry in Westone's Wonder Boy series (Monster World III in Japan), released in 1991.

links.took: Underground tunnel carving, chasing monsters that transform into tunnel-digging forms, and dropping heavy objects to crush pursuers.
links.added: Delivered smooth custom-coded CGA software sprites and pulse-width-modulated PC speaker renditions of 'Popcorn' to become an IBM PC classic.
links.extra: Programmed by Rob Sleath at Canadian developer Windmill Software in 1983.

links.took: Carving custom subterranean pathways through earth layers while dropping overhead boulders onto pursuing creatures.
links.added: Swapped the inflating air pump for a motorized emerald-harvesting digger firing recharging fireballs and collecting shattered gold bags.
links.extra: Synthesized Mr. Do! and Dig Dug for early 4.77 MHz IBM PCs.

links.took: Electronic Arts' licensed NBA star power, authentic player tendencies, and accessible console/PC basketball feel.
links.added: Scaled half-court one-on-one duels with shatterable backboards up to full five-on-five NBA playoff teams and signature moves.

src.t: Wikipedia: One on One: Dr. J vs. Larry Bird
Wikipedia: Lakers versus Celtics and the NBA Playoffs

links.extra: Eric Hammond's 1983 hit launched EA's basketball line, directly spawning Lakers vs. Celtics and later NBA Live.

links.took: Star-driven NBA basketball spectacle spotlighting real player personalities and glass-shattering slam dunks.
links.added: Turned licensed superstar matchups into hyper-kinetic 2-on-2 arcade showdowns with turbo sprints and impossible aerial flips.

src.t: Wikipedia: One on One: Dr. J vs. Larry Bird
MobyGames: One on One: Dr. J vs. Larry Bird

links.extra: Eric Hammond's 1983 EA classic was the first major hit built around real licensed athletes and shattering backboards.

links.took: Electronic Arts' early sports-publishing blueprint combining pro-league authenticity with crisp 16-bit home playability.
links.added: Established EA's NBA Playoff series on PC and Sega Genesis, laying the direct foundation for the long-running NBA Live franchise.

src.t: Wikipedia: Lakers versus Celtics and the NBA Playoffs

links.extra: Designed by Robert Weatherby and Michael Brook for Electronic Arts.

links.took: The Learning Company's playful visual edutainment philosophy teaching core skills through interactive Apple II mini-games.
links.added: Shifted from boolean logic circuits to early-childhood phonics, word sorting, and reading games that spawned a multi-decade educational franchise.
links.extra: Designed by Leslie Grimm at The Learning Company in 1983, one year after Warren Robinett's Rocky's Boots.

links.took: Fast-paced first-person 3D ground-level arena maneuvering with radar awareness of an opposing rival.
links.added: Replaced vector tank battles with split-screen 3D scrolling checkerboard hover-sports, scoring goals with a bouncing plasmorb over an algorithmic jazz soundtrack.
links.extra: Directed by David Levine as one of Lucasfilm Games' two debut commercial titles in 1984.

links.took: Lucasfilm Games' founding culture of custom 8-bit technical experimentation and playful audio-visual craft.
links.added: Pivoted the young studio from groundbreaking 3D action showcases into interactive cinematic storytelling powered by SCUMM.
links.extra: Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus! launched Lucasfilm Games in 1984 before its adventure-game golden age.

links.took: Single-screen ladder climbing and hazard dodging across compact stacked architectural chambers.
links.added: Expanded into a 20-room scrolling kung-fu fortress combining lantern collection, flying kicks, and an asymmetric two-player mode letting a second player control the Green Yamo.
links.extra: Created by Ron Fortier and Kelly Day for Datasoft in 1984 across Atari 8-bit, C64, and Apple II.

links.took: Bruce Artwick's pioneering 3D wireframe flight physics, cockpit instruments, and navigation fundamentals.
links.added: Expanded the simulation with multi-color scenery, four major US flight regions, Piper Archer II instruments, and a full WWI Ace combat mode across Apple II, C64, and Atari.
links.extra: Published by subLOGIC in 1984 as the direct consumer follow-up to Bruce Artwick's 1979 original and MSFS 1.0.

links.took: First-person Atari 8-bit cockpit immersion featuring instrument readouts, target locks, and spatial flight tension.
links.added: Replaced starry space with real-time fractal mountain canyons where players land to pick up downed pilots—and occasionally get startled by alien Jaggi impostors smashing the canopy.
links.extra: Directed by David Fox using Loren Carpenter's Pixar-pioneered fractal terrain algorithm at Lucasfilm Games in 1984.

links.took: David Fox's playful Lucasfilm Games design craft and memorable tongue-in-cheek sci-fi suspense.
links.added: Carried Fox from cockpit fractal exploration into leading SCUMM's globe-trotting alien-conspiracy graphic adventure.

src.t: Wikipedia: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders

links.extra: David Fox served as project leader on both Rescue on Fractalus! (1984) and Zak McKracken (1988).

links.took: First-person illustrated adventure exploration solving a murder mystery across interconnected rooms.
links.added: Replaced typed text parsers with ICOM Simulations' MacVenture windowed point-and-click interface, letting Macintosh players drag objects and click verb buttons directly on noir scenes.

src.t: MobyGames: Deja Vu: A Nightmare Comes True!!

links.extra: Debuted ICOM Simulations' pioneering MacVenture point-and-click UI in 1985.

links.took: ICOM Simulations' MacVenture windowed point-and-click interface, draggable inventory, and clickable compass navigation.
links.added: Transplanted the interface from 1940s detective noir into a perilous fantasy castle packed with lethal traps, burning torches, and memorable death prose.
links.extra: Released on Macintosh in 1987 and widely loved via Kemco's atmospheric 1989 NES conversion.

links.took: First-person static-screen Macintosh adventure design navigating illustrated fantasy environments purely by mouse clicks.
links.added: Stripped away text boxes and verb menus altogether in favor of full-screen pre-rendered 3D worlds and environmental puzzle storytelling.
links.extra: Shadowgate helped establish first-person mouse-driven exploration on the Macintosh six years before Myst.

links.took: Bob Whitehead's clean sports animation craft and readable arcade timing honed during his Activision years.
links.added: Introduced the now-standard behind-the-pitcher broadcast camera angle for baseball video games alongside detailed pitch-selection and defensive positioning.
links.extra: Designed by Activision co-founder Bob Whitehead for Accolade in 1985.

links.took: Behind-the-pitcher broadcast diamond framing paired with real-time arcade batting and pitching timing.
links.added: Fused arcade play with deep statistical managerial simulations, custom stadium physics, and instant replays advised by Hall of Fame manager Earl Weaver.
links.extra: Designed by Eddie Dombrower for Electronic Arts in 1987 on Amiga and DOS.

links.took: Statistically grounded sports simulation driven by historical player ratings, matchups, and strategic play-calling.
links.added: Brought tabletop baseball management math to life with animated Amiga graphics, custom ballpark dimensions, and real-time voice commentary.
links.extra: Widely cited as a landmark bridge between statistical tabletop sims and modern sports video games.

links.took: Atari Games' four-player cooperative arcade dungeon crawling with depleting health, food pickups, and booming voice announcements.
links.added: Allowed multiple players to choose the same hero class in distinct colors while adding ricocheting shots, acid puddles, fire-breathing dragons, and 'It' tag hazards.
links.extra: Direct arcade sequel by Atari Games in 1986.

links.took: The traditional 144-tile Chinese Mahjong tile set of bamboo, characters, dots, winds, and dragons.
links.added: Adapted Brodie Lockard's 1981 PLATO solo tile-matching creation into a massive Activision hit clearing stacked pyramid layers pair by pair.

src.t: Tedium: Brodie Lockard and the Origin of Mahjong Solitaire

links.extra: Stanford gymnast Brodie Lockard coded the original PLATO version with a mouth-stick before Activision published Shanghai in 1986.

links.took: Interplay's six-character first-person party dungeon crawling, bard songs, and animated monster portraits.
links.added: Expanded beyond Skara Brae into a full wilderness overworld connecting six cities, ranged combat distances, and real-time timed death-snare puzzle rooms.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Bard's Tale II: The Destiny Knight

links.extra: Designed by Michael Cranford for Interplay and Electronic Arts in 1986.

links.took: Infocom's Z-machine interactive fiction engine, literary room prose, and rich natural-language text parser.
links.added: Used Infocom's parser to craft Brian Moriarty's acclaimed time-traveling historical fantasy linking world nuclear test sites to the 1945 Trinity detonation.
links.extra: Written by Brian Moriarty at Infocom in 1986; accompanied by a comic book and paper crane feelie.

links.took: Brian Moriarty's poetic fantasy world-building, emotional resonance, and carefully structured narrative puzzles.
links.added: Replaced typed text parsers entirely with a musical four-note distaff interface inside Lucasfilm Games' SCUMM engine.
links.extra: Brian Moriarty left Infocom for Lucasfilm Games, directing Loom in 1990.

links.took: Nintendo's side-view jumping momentum, secret warp zones, trophy/coin gathering, and vibrant obstacle platforming.
links.added: Translated console-style jump-and-collect level design onto Apple II and DOS disk magazines with jetpacks, guns, and lethal traps.

src.t: John Romero, Doom Guy: Life in First Person (2023)

links.extra: John Romero explicitly cited Super Mario Bros. as the direct inspiration for his 1988 UpTime disk-magazine game.

links.took: John Romero's Dangerous Dave sprite and platformer sensibility, placed directly into John Carmack's smooth-scrolling PC Super Mario Bros. 3 demo.
links.added: Turned the 'Dangerous Dave in Copyright Infringement' prototype into an original shareware DOS scrolling trilogy that founded id Software.

src.t: Rock Paper Shotgun: Dangerous Dave & Commander Keen History

links.extra: Carmack and Tom Hall dropped Romero's Dave sprite into their overnight SMB3 scrolling demo in September 1990.

links.took: MicroProse's accessible 3D combat flight modeling and historical Cold War strike missions.
links.added: Introduced radar-cross-section stealth mechanics—managing bay doors, banking angles, and low-altitude terrain masking to slip past enemy SAM grids.
links.extra: Co-designed by Sid Meier and Andy Hollis at MicroProse in 1988.

links.took: Sierra On-Line's animated third-person fairy-tale graphic adventure structure mixing walking controls with text commands.
links.added: Debuted Sierra's high-resolution SCI engine, full sound-card orchestral music, a day-to-night 24-hour clock, and a rare female lead protagonist in Princess Rosella.
links.extra: Designed by Roberta Williams in 1988; launched Sierra's Creative Interpreter (SCI) era.

links.took: Sierra's SCI adventure architecture, orchestral sound-card scores, and sweeping storybook setpieces.
links.added: Replaced the typed text parser completely with an icon-driven 256-color VGA point-and-click interface.
links.extra: Bridged Sierra's parser-driven 1980s hits and its 1990s VGA point-and-click blockbusters.

links.took: Jon Van Caneghem's expansive first-person grid RPG mixing classic fantasy exploration with hidden sci-fi lore.
links.added: Added an automap, two new character classes (Ninja and Barbarian), hirelings, time-travel quests, and battles against up to 255 simultaneous enemies.

src.t: Wikipedia: Might and Magic II: Gates to Another World

links.extra: Developed by New World Computing in 1988.

links.took: FTL Games' real-time first-person grid dungeon crawling, rune-combination spellcasting, and direct mouse object manipulation.
links.added: Delivered a fiendishly non-linear, trap-laden expansion dungeon importing Dungeon Master champions into four interconnected thematic paths.
links.extra: Released by FTL Games in 1989 and famed for its brutal puzzle complexity.

links.took: Grid-based block-pushing logic puzzles where every single tile push can permanently lock or open a solution.
links.added: Injected action-arcade pacing, elemental boots (fire, ice, water, force), patrolling monsters, and 144 compact brain-teasing maps for the Atari Lynx and Windows.
links.extra: Creator Chuck Sommerville explicitly cited Sokoban and Boulder Dash as primary inspirations.

links.took: Collecting scattered gems/chips across hazardous tile grids under strict timing and monster avoidance.
links.added: Combined item-gathering map navigation with Sokoban block puzzles, locked color-coded doors, and clever mechanical tile gadgets.
links.extra: Built at Epyx in roughly ten weeks for the Atari Lynx launch before achieving fame in Microsoft Entertainment Pack 4.

links.took: Cinemaware's 'interactive movie' presentation combining lush Amiga cinema art with genre-blending action mini-games.
links.added: Traded medieval jousting for a 1950s giant-ant B-movie sci-fi thriller where a geologist races a 15-day clock across a desert town via interviews, hospital escapes, and aerial spraying.

src.t: Wikipedia: It Came from the Desert
MobyGames: It Came from the Desert

links.extra: Designed by Greg Malone for Cinemaware on Amiga in 1989.

links.took: Addictive real-time falling-block arcade pressure requiring rapid spatial planning as drop speeds accelerate.
links.added: Created directly after Atari Games' Tetris rights dispute, pivoting from shape-fitting to catching colored tiles on a paddle and stacking horizontal, vertical, and diagonal color matches.

src.t: Mark Stephen Pierce & Dave Akers Retrospectives

links.extra: Atari Games provocatively marketed Klax in 1989-1990 with the tagline 'More Fun Than Tetris!'.

links.took: Mark Crowe and Scott Murphy's comedic sci-fi misadventures starring hapless janitor Roger Wilco.
links.added: Upgraded to Sierra's SCI engine with a landmark Roland MT-32 soundtrack by Bob Siebenberg, a meta-satire rescue of the Two Guys from Andromeda, and an arcade Astro Chicken mini-game.
links.extra: Released by Sierra On-Line in 1989 and widely celebrated as an early PC sound-card showcase.

links.took: Single-screen overhead multi-wheel arcade racing around compact twisting circuits with cash wrench upgrades.
links.added: Moved racing onto bumpy mud tracks with jump hills, boostable nitro bursts, four-player steering cabinets, and post-race cash upgrades for shocks, tires, and acceleration.
links.extra: Developed by Leland Corporation in 1989 endorsing off-road champion Ivan 'Ironman' Stewart.

links.took: Compact arena dirt racing paired with post-race cash upgrades for engines, tires, suspension, and boost.
links.added: Shifted the view to scrolling isometric alien tracks armed with missiles, mines, licensed rock MIDI tracks, and loud announcer calls.
links.extra: Carried Super Off Road's addicting race-and-upgrade arcade loop into Silicon & Synapse's 1993 classic.

links.took: Distinctive Software's dashboard-cockpit exotic sports car racing evading highway traffic and police cruisers.
links.added: Added head-to-head racing against a computer rival (Ferrari F40 vs. Porsche 959), varied scenery hazards, and official add-on car and scenery disks.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Duel: Test Drive II
MobyGames: The Duel: Test Drive II

links.extra: Developed by Distinctive Software and published by Accolade in 1989.

links.took: Distinctive Software's exotic supercar rivalry, cockpit instrumentation, scenic point-to-point highways, and police chases.
links.added: Carried the same Vancouver team—by then acquired as EA Canada—into 3D texture-mapped sports-car racing created with Road & Track magazine.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Duel: Test Drive II

links.extra: Electronic Arts bought Distinctive Software in 1991, turning it into EA Canada.

links.took: Branching LaserDisc full-motion video playback reacting instantaneously to split-second player inputs.
links.added: Replaced animated cartoon timing prompts with live-action Western actors and a cabinet light gun for quick-draw cowboy shootouts.
links.extra: Created by American Laser Games in 1990 using live-action footage filmed in New Mexico.

links.took: Arcade light-gun reaction shooting popping out live enemies from cover windows and penalizing shots against innocent bystanders.
links.added: Replaced pre-filmed LaserDisc clips with real-time 3D polygonal environments, target lock-on reticles, and location-based enemy damage.
links.extra: Demonstrated mainstream arcade appetite for dramatic reaction-based light-gun shootouts.

links.took: id Software's smooth EGA side-scrolling PC engine, pogo-stick traversal, and episode-based shareware distribution.
links.added: Upgraded to Carmack's CRTC full-screen omnidirectional scrolling, 2.5D sloped perspective tiles, swimming stages, and a lush animated overworld map.

src.t: Wikipedia: Commander Keen in Goodbye, Galaxy

links.extra: Released by id Software via Apogee in December 1991 as the first half of Goodbye, Galaxy!

links.took: Apogee Software's three-episode shareware PC side-scrolling distribution model and brisk DOS action-platformer appeal.
links.added: Swapped a child astronaut for a brash action-movie hero blasting Dr. Proton's techbots, shooting destructible crates, and climbing ledges across futuristic cities.
links.extra: Programmed by Todd Replogle for Apogee Software in July 1991.

links.took: Apogee's wisecracking action-hero protagonist, futuristic urban sci-fi mayhem, and interactive destructible props.
links.added: Catapulted the 2D DOS side-scroller mascot into 3D Realms' Build-engine first-person shooter packed with voice one-liners, jetpacks, and interactive real-world locales.
links.extra: Todd Replogle programmed both the original 1991 platformer and the landmark 1996 FPS.

links.took: Westwood's real-time first-person AD&D grid dungeon crawling, four-character party formation, and clickable combat hands.
links.added: Opened up the claustrophobic sewers with an outdoor forest entrance, deeper NPC dialogue trees, larger multi-tower dungeons, and an actual cinematic ending.

src.t: Wikipedia: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon
MobyGames: Eye of the Beholder II

links.extra: Developed by Westwood Associates for SSI in 1991.

links.took: Westwood's smooth real-time first-person party RPG framework, lush painted environments, and conversational encounters.
links.added: Dropped complex AD&D rules for an original streamlined fantasy setting featuring Patrick Stewart's voice acting and an automatic mapping system.

src.t: Wikipedia: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon
Wikipedia: Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos

links.extra: Westwood built Lands of Lore directly after parting ways with SSI following Eye of the Beholder II.

links.took: Will Wright and Maxis's open-ended systemic simulation toy philosophy modeling living ecosystems without rigid scripts.
links.added: Zoomed from planetary Gaia dynamics down to a backyard ant colony, letting players guide black ants against red rivals via digging tunnels and laying pheromone trails.

src.t: Game Developer: Will Wright SimAnt Retrospective

links.extra: Co-designed by Will Wright and Justin McCormick in 1991, inspired by myrmecologist E. O. Wilson.

links.took: Distributed agent navigation driven by environmental pheromone trails that pull autonomous ants toward food or threats.
links.added: Reimagined pheromone trails as smart-object 'advertisements' broadcasting hunger, comfort, and fun signals that guide simulated people around a suburban home.

src.t: Game Developer: Will Wright on SimAnt & The Sims AI

links.extra: Will Wright directly adapted SimAnt's emergent pheromone behavior into the needs-advertising AI powering The Sims.

links.took: Mounted arcade machine-gun rail shooting spraying down waves of advancing enemies while conserving secondary explosives.
links.added: Upgraded to dual recoil-vibrating positional guns, digitized live-action film sprites, and limb-destructible T-800 endoskeletons.
links.extra: Designed by George Petro and Jack Haeger at Midway in 1991.

links.took: Origin Systems' cinematic space-combat carrier narrative, branching mission trees, and sprite-scaled dogfights.
links.added: Added a darker overarching betrayal storyline, heavy torpedo bombers, gun turrets, and full digitized cockpit voice acting via its optional Speech Accessory Pack.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi

links.extra: Produced by Chris Roberts and directed by Ellen Guon and Stephen Beeman at Origin Systems in 1991.

links.took: Origin's voice-acted space opera storytelling, recurring wingman drama, and escalating war against the Kilrathi Empire.
links.added: Replaced pixel cutscenes and sprite fighters with texture-mapped 3D polygon spacecraft and live-action FMV starring Mark Hamill.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi

links.extra: Bridged the original 2D bitmap space sims and Origin's blockbuster CD-ROM FMV era.

links.took: Illustrated British computer text adventures pairing atmospheric room artwork with a rich full-sentence verb parser.
links.added: Set a 16-bit benchmark on Atari ST and Amiga with lush hand-drawn scrolled illustrations, witty surrealism, and Magnetic Scrolls' celebrated parser.
links.extra: Developed by Magnetic Scrolls in 1986; widely praised for advancing graphical text-adventure craft in Britain.

links.took: Blade Runner-inspired cyberpunk detective storytelling pairing grim neon atmosphere with menu-driven investigation.
links.added: Brought hand-painted digitized VGA art, first-person point-and-click exploration, real-time passage of days, and branching consequences to DOS and Amiga.
links.extra: Developed by Dynamix in 1990 using its Dynamix Game Development System (DGDS).

links.took: Four-character real-time party RPG combat, inventory management, and first-person spatial exploration.
links.added: Moved party adventuring out of grid corridors onto a free-roaming solid-polygon 3D island with dynamic day-night skies and rising celestial constellation bosses.
links.extra: Developed by French studio Infogrames in 1989 and widely ported to SNES.

links.took: Epyx's multi-event international sports anthology pairing distinct control schemes with ceremonial medal standings.
links.added: Stepped outside traditional Olympics into eight regional folk and extreme sports including Scottish caber toss, sumo wrestling, cliff diving, and bull riding.
links.extra: Released by Epyx in 1986 between Winter Games and California Games.

links.took: Epyx's lighthearted, non-Olympic anthology format spotlighting quirky regional sports with expressive animations.
links.added: Focused the multi-event formula squarely on West Coast youth culture—half-pipe skateboarding, footbag, surfing, BMX, and flying disc.
links.extra: Bridged Epyx's Olympic-style Games entries and its iconic 1987 California Games hit.

links.took: MECC's classroom-tested Apple II educational design turning school drills into gripping, replayable arcade loops.
links.added: Built a fast-paced grid-eating math chase where players munch multiples, primes, and factors while dodging roaming Troggles.
links.extra: Created by MECC in 1986 and distributed across thousands of North American school computer labs.

links.took: Broderbund's side-scrolling aircraft sortie loop launching from a home base to strike enemy installations and return safely.
links.added: Swapped the rescue helicopter for a WWII carrier-based F6F Hellcat strafing bunkers, dropping bombs, and launching torpedoes against Pacific fleet targets.
links.extra: Designed by Steve Waldo and published by Broderbund in 1989 (originally developed on Apple II and famed on Amiga).

links.took: Elevator-linked subterranean sci-fi base exploration hunting room passcodes to disable a doomsday computer before time expires.
links.added: Paired Sega's Master System run-and-gun laser combat with three swappable anime agents unlocking distinct paths across a massive interconnected alien fortress.
links.extra: Developed by Sega in 1987 as a tie-in to the Tatsunoko anime, starring Opa-Opa as a cameo.

links.took: Precise single-screen action-platforming navigating hazards, ropes, and switches through treacherous multi-room strongholds.
links.added: Combined razor-sharp monochrome Macintosh animation, digitized sound effects, and mouse-aimed rock-throwing trajectories to bring tactile arcade action to the Mac.
links.extra: Programmed by Jonathan Gay (who later co-created Flash) for Silicon Beach Software in 1986.

links.took: Pure two-paddle ball-deflection rally gameplay built on angle control and reflex counter-strikes.
links.added: Shifted to a first-person mouse-controlled sci-fi cantina air-hockey table featuring nine eccentric alien opponents with signature curve shots and personalities.
links.extra: Created by Christopher Gross for Broderbund in 1989 on Macintosh before popular Amiga and Atari ST ports.

links.took: Games Workshop's Old World fantasy archetypes—Barbarian, Dwarf, Elf, and Wizard—battling Orcs, Fimir, and Chaos Warriors.
links.added: Translated the hit tabletop dungeon-crawl board game onto home computers with an isometric 3D board, turn-based corridor fog-of-war, and treasure deck draws.
links.extra: Developed by Gremlin Graphics in 1991 from Games Workshop and Milton Bradley's 1989 board game.

links.took: Fast, responsive arcade soccer built around crisp passing chains, sliding tackles, and diving goalkeeper saves.
links.added: Pivoted to a vertical behind-the-goal Mode 7 SNES perspective that became an early showcase for 16-bit console sports.
links.extra: Developed by Human Entertainment in 1991 (Super Formation Soccer in Japan).

links.took: Accessible 16-bit SNES arcade soccer gameplay balancing quick dribbling, power shots, and tournament progression.
links.added: Elevated console soccer with richly animated side-view matches, distinct player appearances, and deep tactical formations.
links.extra: Super Soccer set the early SNES soccer benchmark prior to Konami's 1994 classic.

links.took: Real-time economic management juggling competing rivals, budgets, and scheduling efficiency.
links.added: Placed management inside an animated cross-section TV skyscraper where players run elevators to license films, book ad contracts, and beat rival stations in nightly ratings.
links.extra: Developed by Rainbow Arts in Germany in 1991; beloved European PC/Amiga cult tycoon classic.

links.took: Sega's lush 16-bit Disney platforming animation, expressive sprite humor, and crisp Mega Drive control.
links.added: Gave Donald Duck a globe-trotting Indiana Jones-style treasure hunt letting players pick destinations by plane and scale walls using upgraded plunger guns.
links.extra: Developed in-house by Sega in 1991 immediately following Castle of Illusion.

links.took: Capcom's nonlinear boss-select run-and-gun structure stealing defeated Robot Masters' signature weapons.
links.added: Condensed iconic NES Robot Masters from Mega Man 1 and 2 onto the Game Boy while introducing the original Mega Man Killer rival, Enker.

src.t: Wikipedia: Mega Man: Dr. Wily's Revenge
MobyGames: Mega Man: Dr. Wily's Revenge

links.extra: Developed by Minakuchi Engineering for Capcom in 1991 as Mega Man's handheld debut.

links.took: Snappy NES run-jump momentum, colorful themed stage maps, and selectable power-up traversal abilities.
links.added: Recast the template around Buster Bunny teaming up with swappable animal pals (Plucky Duck, Dizzy Devil, Furrball) in one of Konami's slickest late-NES platformers.
links.extra: Released by Konami in 1991 and widely distributed on NES and Dendy.

links.took: Capcom's CPS-1 arcade side-scrolling combat feel, huge enemy sprites, and three-player co-op crowd management.
links.added: Blended belt-scrolling action with five distinct fantasy RPG classes (Fighter, Cleric, Elf, Wizard, Dwarf), shield blocking, and persistent weapon-and-armor level upgrades.
links.extra: Released by Capcom in 1991; paved the way for Capcom's licensed Dungeons & Dragons arcade beat-'em-ups.

links.took: Al Lowe's comedic adult graphic adventure starring luckless lounge lizard Larry Laffer.
links.added: Transitioned the series to Sierra's higher-resolution SCI engine and broadened the setting into a globe-trotting James Bond parody across cruise ships and tropical islands.

src.t: Wikipedia: Leisure Suit Larry Goes Looking for Love (in Several Wrong Places)

links.extra: Designed by Al Lowe at Sierra On-Line in 1988.

links.took: Magnetic Fields' top-down Amiga combat racing buying missiles, armor, and turbo upgrades between heats.
links.added: Added simultaneous two-player split-screen racing, bridge jumps, train crossings, homing weapons, and tongue-in-cheek championship quiz dilemmas.
links.extra: Programmed by Shaun Southern at Magnetic Fields and published by Gremlin Graphics in 1991.

links.took: Konami's deliberate whip-cracking gothic action-platforming, candle pickups, and Dracula-hunting Belmont lineage.
links.added: Adapted the series to the Game Boy with Christopher Belmont's fireball-launching upgraded whip and tense rope-climbing gauntlets.
links.extra: Konami's 1989 portable debut for Castlevania.

links.took: First Star Software's simultaneous split-screen slapstick sabotage rigging hidden traps against a rival spy.
links.added: Moved the duel out of a multi-room embassy onto a tropical volcanic island packed with pit traps, shark hazards, and missile parts needed to assemble a submarine.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spy vs. Spy II: The Island Caper

links.extra: Developed by First Star Software in 1985 based on MAD Magazine's iconic comic strip.

links.took: Epyx's somersaulting spy platforming, digitized speech, and puzzle-piece decryption inside Elvin Atombender's lair.
links.added: Expanded the base into eight distinct themed towers connected by subways, adding safecracking, time bombs, and tape-recording musical lock puzzles.
links.extra: Developed by Novotrade and published by Epyx in 1988.
